question: In 2005 the world’s countries averaged 0.643 on V-Dem’s Academic Freedom Index (0 = none, 1 = full), which asks whether scholars can freely research, teach and publish. What was the average in 2025?
indicator: V-Dem Academic Freedom Index (average of the world’s countries; 0 = none, 1 = full)
why: In the late 1980s the index rose fast, from 0.448 in 1985 to 0.545 in 1990, and peaked in 2005. It held near that level for almost a decade, began to fall in the mid-2010s, and has fallen fastest in recent years: 0.622 in 2019, 0.549 in 2025. So the average country is back roughly where it was in 1990.

question: How common are teenage births today?
indicator: Teen births (ages 15-19)
why: Girls staying in school longer, wider access to contraception, and later marriage cut the global teen birth rate from 92 to 38 per 1,000. Still, about 12 million girls aged 15-19 give birth every year, mostly in lower-income countries, and in Sub-Saharan Africa the rate remains roughly 2.5 times the world average.

question: Is global literacy rising?
indicator: Adult literacy
why: Reading is the precondition for learning, work, and using public services. The global aggregate partly relies on modeled or carried-forward country estimates where annual surveys don't exist, so progress is real but not annually measured everywhere.

question: Is adult obesity rising?
indicator: Adult obesity worldwide
why: Adult obesity has been climbing for over three decades with no sign of slowing: age-standardised prevalence among adults 18+ rose from 6.1% in 1990 to 16.4% in 2024 — roughly one adult in six. But for the first time, this is tracked through consistent global monitoring (222 million children, adolescents, and adults measured across 200 countries) and matched by genuinely effective medical treatments that didn’t exist a decade ago.

question: What area of land do the world’s fields and pastures cover?
indicator: Agricultural land: cropland, permanent crops, meadows and pastures (world, billion hectares)
why: For centuries humanity grew more food mostly by ploughing up new land. But around 2001 the world’s area of fields and pastures stopped growing: it peaked at 4.87 billion hectares then and stood at 4.80 billion in 2023, almost 75 million hectares less. Meanwhile the value of farm output in constant prices grew almost one and a half times: farms produce more from the same land. Still, agriculture occupies 37% of the planet’s land area.

why: In eight years the number of scholarly works about AI — journal articles, conference papers, preprints — tripled, from 139 thousand in 2016 to 423 thousand in 2024. question: How many passengers flew with India’s airlines in 2023?
indicator: Passengers carried by airlines registered in India (domestic and international flights, millions per year)
why: Low-cost airlines, which appeared in India in the 2000s, made flying affordable for millions of people: the country’s airlines carried 17 million passengers in 2000, 167 million in 2019 and, after the pandemic slump (69 million in 2020), 180 million in 2023. Still, for 1.44 billion people that is only about one trip for every eight people a year.

question: How many passengers did airlines in Sub-Saharan Africa carry in 2023?
indicator: Passengers carried by airlines registered in Sub-Saharan Africa (millions per year)
why: As the region’s cities and economies grow, more and more people fly: local airlines carried 4.6 million passengers in 1970, 17.9 million in 2000 and 66.2 million in 2019. The pandemic cut that to 24.5 million in 2020. But the recovery is not complete: 57 million in 2023, noticeably fewer than before the pandemic.

question: How many passengers did the world’s airlines carry in 2023?
indicator: Airline passengers, domestic and international flights (world, billions per year)
why: In half a century flying stopped being only for the rich: the world’s airlines carried 0.31 billion passengers in 1970 and 4.46 billion in 2019. The pandemic cut that to 1.77 billion in 2020, but by 2023 it had almost recovered, to 4.27 billion. These are trips, not people, though: someone who flies often is counted many times.

question: What share of seats on passenger planes is taken by paying passengers?
indicator: Airline passenger load factor (world, share of seats filled by paying passengers)
why: Airlines have learned to fill their planes: paying passengers took 60.9% of seats in 1950, only 54.1% in 1971, and 83.2% in 2024 — more than in any year on record. A fuller plane burns less fuel per passenger. The figure is fragile, though: in 2020, when the pandemic stopped travel, it fell to 65%.

question: How many litres of pure alcohol does the average person aged 15 or over in the world drink in a year?
indicator: Alcohol consumption (world, litres of pure alcohol per person aged 15+ per year, WHO estimates)
why: This counts everything — beer, wine and spirits, legal and illicit — converted into pure alcohol. From 2000 to 2012 consumption rose from 5.1 to 5.9 litres, then began to fall: 5.4 litres in 2019. The latest estimate, 4.9 litres, is for 2020 — the first year of the pandemic — so whether that level holds will show in the next data.

question: What share of the world’s women have anaemia?
indicator: Prevalence of anaemia among women aged 15–49 (world)
why: Anaemia is a shortage of haemoglobin in the blood; its most common cause is too little iron in the diet. It leaves women tired more quickly and makes pregnancy riskier. Until 2012 its prevalence slowly fell, from 29.4% to 27.6%, but it has been rising since: 30.7% in 2023. In South Asia more than half of women have anaemia (51.1%). In 2012 WHO member states set a goal of halving it by 2025, but the world has only moved further away from that goal.

question: What was the average size of the ozone hole over Antarctica in September–October 2025?
indicator: Antarctic ozone hole area (average for 7 September – 13 October, million km²)
why: The ozone hole is the area over Antarctica where the ozone layer thins sharply each southern spring. It appeared in the late 1970s and grew fast, from 0.1 million km² in 1979 to over 22 million in the early 1990s. The 1987 Montreal Protocol wound down production of ozone-depleting substances, but they linger in the atmosphere for decades, so the hole peaked only in 2006, at 26.6 million km². Since then it has generally been smaller, but not every year: 25.6 million km² in 2015 and above 23 million each year from 2020 to 2023, then 18.7 million in 2025.

question: What volume of fish, shellfish and seaweed do the world’s farms produce in a year?
indicator: Aquaculture: fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants grown on farms (world, million tonnes)
why: While the wild catch has stalled, farms at sea, in ponds and in tanks have raised output from 2 million tonnes in 1960 to 141 million in 2024, more than the entire wild catch (94.4 million tonnes). Almost six in every ten tonnes are farmed in China (82 million). The total includes seaweed, though, and part of the farmed fish is fed on feed made from wild fish, so aquaculture does not fully take the pressure off the seas.

question: What area does Arctic sea ice cover in September, when it is at its smallest?
indicator: Arctic sea ice extent in September (monthly average, million km²)
why: Satellites have tracked Arctic ice since the late 1970s. In September 1979, at the end of the summer melt, the ice covered 7.05 million km². The record low came in 2012: 3.57 million km². There has been no new record since (4.81 million km² in 2026), but no return to the levels of the 1980s and 1990s either: since 2007 the September ice has never exceeded 5.3 million km².

question: How much CO₂ does aviation emit per passenger per kilometre?
indicator: Aviation CO₂ emissions per passenger-kilometre (world, grams)
why: More efficient engines, lighter aircraft and fuller cabins cut emissions per passenger-kilometre by more than half: from 357 grams in 1990 to 157 grams in 2019, the last year before the pandemic. But people fly so much more that aviation’s total CO₂ emissions almost doubled over the same period, from 0.54 to 1.03 billion tonnes.

question: How many people have basic sanitation?
indicator: Basic sanitation access
why: Sustained WASH programs and SDG monitoring expanded household toilets and sewerage, lifting coverage from 54.8% in 2000 to about four in five people. Yet roughly 1.5 billion still lack even a basic toilet, and much of what counts as «basic» is still not safely managed.

question: How much does a lithium-ion battery cell cost per kilowatt-hour of storage?
indicator: Price of lithium-ion battery cells (world, $ per kWh of capacity, 2024 dollars)
why: As production grew — first for phones and laptops, then for electric cars — lithium-ion cells became more than 100 times cheaper: from $9,210 per kilowatt-hour of capacity in 1991 to $78 in 2024 (in 2024 dollars, i.e. adjusted for inflation). question: What percentage of children under 5 in Nepal had their birth registered in 2019?
indicator: Share of children under 5 whose birth is registered (Nepal)
why: A birth record is the basis of a child’s legal identity. In 2006 only 35% of Nepal’s under-fives had one; in 2019, 77.2% did. Progress was not even: between the 2014 and 2016 surveys the rate even dipped slightly, from 58.1% to 56.2%. A new national survey in 2024–2025 found 85.4%, and a review of its results credits the Child Grant programme, which gives families a financial incentive to register their children. Still, about one child under five in seven has no birth record.

question: What share of births in Rwanda are attended by a doctor, nurse or midwife?
indicator: Births attended by skilled health staff (Rwanda)
why: In 2000 only about one birth in three in Rwanda was attended by a doctor, nurse or midwife; in 2020, 94.2%. The country trained community health workers in every village to follow pregnant women and help them reach a health centre, introduced community-based health insurance and began paying clinics extra for births delivered there. But the indicator counts only whether a skilled attendant was present, not the quality of care: complicated births also need well-equipped hospitals.

question: Of every 100 babies born in the world, how many are born with a doctor, nurse or midwife present?
indicator: Births attended by skilled health staff (world)
why: In Gapminder’s 2019 survey with Ipsos MORI (about 15,500 people in 31 countries), the most common answer was “30%”, lower even than the share in 2000 (62%); in 2019 it was 83.3%. The rise sped up after 2010: by 7.5 percentage points in 2000–2010 and by 13.8 in 2010–2019. Gapminder links the rise to the targets the UN set for reducing the number of women who die in childbirth. But about one birth in six still takes place without a trained health worker, and the world figure rests on only three estimates: 2000, 2010 and 2019.

question: In 1960 about 100,000 black rhinos lived in Africa. How many were there in 2021?
indicator: Number of black rhinos (world)
why: In the 1970s demand for rhino horn soared, and poachers cut the population to 14,785 animals by 1980 and 2,410 by 1995, 98% below the 1960 estimate. Since then protection has been stepped up and rhinos have been returned to parks in Malawi, Zambia, Botswana and Rwanda. Numbers have more than doubled, to 6,195 in 2021, yet that is about 6% of the 1960 estimate.

question: Since the 1993 peak, have domestic burglaries in England and Wales fallen by a quarter, by half, or by more? How many thousand were there in 2025?
indicator: Domestic burglary, including attempts (England and Wales, thousands a year, household survey)
why: Since the 1993 peak, domestic burglaries in England and Wales have fallen sixfold, from 2.4 million to 398,000 in 2025. British criminologists who studied the survey for 1992–2012 concluded there is strong evidence that better home security caused the decline, with sturdy locks combined with security lighting working best. The flip side: homes without such protection now face a disproportionately higher risk.

question: What share of laying hens in Czechia live outside cages?
indicator: Share of laying hens in cage-free systems, barns and free range (Czechia)
why: In 2013–2018 between 15% and 17% of Czech laying hens lived without cages. Then the share climbed fast: 32.4% in 2020 and 57.2% in 2025. In 2020 the Czech parliament voted to ban cages for laying hens from 2027, going further than EU rules. The share is rising well ahead of that deadline.

why: Spain shows what the EU’s 2012 cage rule did not change. It banned barren battery cages but still allows larger ‘enriched’ ones, and in Spain those remained the norm: in 2013–2016 only about 7 in 100 laying hens lived without cages. Since then the share has risen almost every year, reaching 40.2% in 2025. Still, most Spanish hens are kept in cages.

question: How many kilocalories of food a day are there per person in Africa?
indicator: Food supply (Africa, kcal per person per day)
why: Until 2010 there was more and more food per person in Africa, from 1,993 to 2,549 kcal a day. Since then the figure has barely moved: 2,556 kcal in 2023. For comparison, in 1961 Asia had even less food per person than Africa (1,805 kcal); now it has 2,991 kcal. And an average hides inequality: better-off families have food to spare, while the poorest get far less.

question: How many cars per 100,000 people were stolen in the US in 2024, after 659 in 1991?
indicator: Motor vehicle theft (US, per 100,000 people, police-reported)
why: The US is an interesting contrast to Britain: it never made electronic immobilisers mandatory, but carmakers fitted them anyway — by about 2006 half of US cars had one, according to a UK Home Office study. Thefts fell threefold between 1991 and 2019, from 659 to 221 per 100,000. Then came a reversal: by 2023 the rate had risen by almost half, to 321. One known cause was Hyundai and Kia models with a mechanical key and no immobiliser, whose weakness spread through TikTok videos in 2022; after software fixes and new immobilisers, the rate fell to 259 in 2024.

why: Denmark was one of the first countries to bet on wind, and wind farms now produce 57.7% of its electricity. question: What share of the world’s CO₂ emissions carries a price, through a carbon tax or an emissions trading system?

question: In 1952, 525 in every 100,000 people in Finland died of heart and blood vessel diseases (age-adjusted). How many in 2024?
indicator: Cardiovascular disease death rate (Finland, per 100,000, age-standardised)
why: In the early 1970s Finnish men died of heart disease more often than anywhere else in the world. In 1972 a project began in the province of North Karelia that, together with communities, shops and food producers, helped people eat less salt and butter and more vegetables, and helped them quit smoking. The approach was spread to the whole country, and later modern treatment of heart attacks and strokes added to the gains. The death rate fell from 489 in 1972 to 102 in 2024. But in 2019–2023 the decline almost stopped (112 and 110), and only the latest year showed a new fall.

A 2020 study found that the decline began in the 1950s and 1960s, decades before the outbreaks of coral disease and bleaching usually blamed for it; the causes named include overfishing, pollution, sea urchin and coral disease, and climate change. question: What share of the world’s people live in households that spend more than a tenth of their budget on health care?
indicator: Share of the population whose household spends more than 10% of its total spending or income on health (world)
why: This is money people pay out of their own pockets: for medicines, doctor visits and hospital care. When it takes more than a tenth of the budget, a family often has to cut back on food or schooling. Health services reached more people over these years, but in many countries patients still pay for much of it themselves: the share of people with such costs did not fall but rose, from 9.6% in 2000 to 13.5% in 2019. question: What was Mexico’s cervical cancer death rate in 2022 — per 100,000 women (age-adjusted)?
indicator: Cervical cancer death rate among women (Mexico, per 100,000 women, age-standardised)
why: In the late 1980s cervical cancer was the leading cause of cancer death among women in Mexico: 18 per 100,000 in 1989. This cancer develops over years, so it can be found and treated while it is still a change in the cells. From the 1990s the country expanded free screening — the Pap smear and later the test for human papillomavirus (HPV) — and by 2022 the death rate had fallen to 5.8, though since 2016 (6.6) it has dropped by less than one point. HPV vaccination of girls, which Mexico introduced in the 2010s, will show up in death rates only many years from now.

question: In 1880 Kyoto’s cherry trees reached full bloom, on average, on day 106 of the year (16 April). On which day of the year do they bloom now, on average?
indicator: Day of the year of peak cherry blossom in Kyoto (30-year average)
change: from day 106 to day 94 of the year (1880–2026)
why: Kyoto’s records of cherry blossom go back to the year 812. The 30-year average date barely moved until the mid-20th century: day 106 in 1880, day 103 in 1950. Since then flowering has shifted to day 94 (4 April). Single years have twice beaten the record set in 1409 (day 86): 2021 (26 March, day 85) and 2023 (25 March, day 84). A study co-authored by the UK Met Office links this to human influence, through climate change and urban warming.

question: Australia’s injury death rate for children aged 1–4 barely moved from 1950 to the mid-1970s. What was it in 2024, per 100,000?
indicator: Death rate from unintentional injuries among children aged 1–4 (Australia, deaths per 100,000 children of that age)
why: For a quarter of a century, from 1950 to the mid-1970s, the injury death rate of young children in Australia barely changed, staying above 30 per 100,000. Since then it has fallen almost tenfold, to 3.7 in 2024. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare names child-resistant containers, seatbelts and pool fencing among the ways to prevent childhood injury, and Royal Life Saving links the decline in child drownings to pool-fencing laws and adult-supervision campaigns. But the gains are unevenly shared: in 2012–2016 Indigenous children under 15 died from injuries at 5.7 times the rate of other children.

question: Out of 100 babies under six months in Sri Lanka, how many were fed only breast milk at the latest survey?
indicator: Exclusive breastfeeding of infants under 6 months (Sri Lanka)
why: Breast milk alone — no other food, not even water — protects babies from diarrhoea and infections in their first six months. In 1987 only 10.2% of babies in Sri Lanka were fed this way; in 2016, 80.9%. Public health midwives visit mothers at home, the country restricted the marketing of infant formula, and maternity hospitals help mothers start breastfeeding in the first hours after birth. indicator: Exoplanets discovered by the transit method (world, cumulative)
why: Most planets found by the transit method were discovered by NASA’s Kepler space telescope (2009–2018): after large batches of confirmations the count rose from 360 in 2013 to 2,689 in 2016. The TESS telescope, launched in 2018, carries on the work, and counting all methods 6,070 exoplanets were known in 2025. question: How many people in East Asia and the Pacific live in extreme poverty?
indicator: Number of people living on less than $3 a day (East Asia and Pacific, millions)
why: In 1990, 1,218 million people in the region that includes China, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines lived on less than $3 a day. Growing industry and cities, where better jobs appeared, cut that number by more than 1.1 billion in three decades: by 2024, 47 million remained in extreme poverty. question: How many people in Sub-Saharan Africa live in extreme poverty?
indicator: Number of people living on less than $3 a day (Sub-Saharan Africa, millions)
why: The share of people in extreme poverty in the region has fallen, from 61.5% in 1990 to 45% in 2024. But the population grew faster than poverty shrank, so the number of people living on less than $3 a day rose from 321 to 581 million. question: What share of people in Indonesia live in extreme poverty?
indicator: Share of people living on less than $3 a day (Indonesia)
why: Poverty in Indonesia retreated, came back and retreated again. After the crisis, growth did most of the work, and from 2007 a cash-transfer programme for poor families added support: by 2025 extreme poverty was down to 3.7%. indicator: Death rate from falls (world, deaths per 100,000 people, not age-adjusted)
why: The world’s death rate from falls is rising: from 6.95 to 9.38 per 100,000 between 2000 and 2021. Population ageing explains part of it: by WHO’s estimate, 71% of fall deaths in 2023 were among people aged 60 and over, and there are more of them every year. Still, WHO stresses that falls among older people can be prevented: balance and strength exercise, checking homes for hazards, and reviewing prescribed medicines.

question: Out of every 100 workers in the world, how many work in farming, forestry or fishing?
indicator: Share of employment in agriculture, forestry and fishing (world)
why: Tractors, fertiliser and better crop varieties let fewer people grow more food, while millions of others moved into factories, construction and services. In 34 years agriculture’s share of employment fell from 42.8% to 25.8%, although in Sub-Saharan Africa almost half of all workers still work the land: 49.3%. And the shift has slowed: since 2015 the share has dropped by less than 3 points, against 6.7 points in the nine years before.

question: How many dollars of value did the average farm worker in the world add in 2025?
indicator: Value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing (world, 2015 US dollars)
why: From 1991 to 2025 value added per worker in agriculture, forestry and fishing worldwide almost tripled, from $1,475 to $4,264 (in 2015 dollars). question: By the best estimate, how many farmed fish are killed for food worldwide each year?
indicator: Farmed fish killed for food per year (world, billions; midpoint of the estimate)
why: Fish are usually counted in tonnes, which hides how many individual animals that is. Fishcount’s estimate converts farm output into numbers of fish: about 13 billion in 1990 and 134 billion in 2022. The uncertainty is large, from 86 to 185 billion for 2022, because the weight of fish at harvest is known only roughly. Fish farming made it possible to produce more fish without a bigger wild catch; this estimate shows how many individual animals lie behind that growth. The estimate also leaves out fish that die on farms before harvest and wild fish caught to make feed.

question: Take the EU’s common farmland birds in 2000 as 100: in 1990 the index stood at 115. Where was it in 2024?
indicator: Populations of common farmland bird species (EU-27, index, 2000 = 100)
why: Skylarks, grey partridges and other birds of fields and meadows have been declining in the EU year after year: the index fell from 115 in 1990 to 68 in 2024, by about two fifths. Forest birds tell a different story: their index dropped from 106 in 1990 to 93 in 2010 and has since recovered to 98. Ecologists link the farmland decline mainly to more intensive agriculture, above all the use of pesticides and fertilisers, and to the loss of fallow land, which leaves birds less food and fewer nesting places. The index is smoothed, so it shows the long-term trend rather than swings between single years.

indicator: World’s fastest supercomputer (operations per second)
why: Ever denser chips, huge numbers of processor cores working in parallel and graphics accelerators made the fastest supercomputer more than 14 million times more powerful: from 124 billion operations per second in 1993 to 1.8 quintillion in 2025. question: How many fatal airliner accidents are there per million commercial flights?
indicator: Fatal airliner accidents per million flights (world, passenger and cargo airliners)
why: More reliable engines, collision-warning systems, pilot simulators and a careful investigation of every crash made flying far safer: in 1970 there were 6.46 fatal accidents per million commercial flights, in 2022 there were 0.48 — more than 13 times fewer. indicator: Female labor force participation

question: How many children does a woman in Bangladesh have on average?
indicator: Total fertility rate (Bangladesh, children per woman)
why: In the early 1970s a woman in Bangladesh had almost seven children on average. In less than 30 years the number more than halved: from 6.51 in 1978 to 2.76 in 2006. A national family-planning programme played a big part: female health workers went door to door, giving advice and bringing contraceptives, while more and more children survived to adulthood. Since then the fall has levelled off: 2.23 in 2015 and 2.14 in 2024, about the replacement level, at which a population holds steady without migration (about 2.17 children per woman for Bangladesh).

question: What was South Korea’s fertility rate in 2024?
indicator: Total fertility rate (South Korea, children per woman)
why: In 1960 a woman in South Korea had almost six children on average (5.99); by 1987, just 1.53. That fall came with rapid development: children survived, and schooling and incomes rose. But fertility did not stop at replacement level, the rate at which a population holds steady without migration (about 2.09 children per woman for Korea), and in 2023 it dropped to 0.72. Researchers point to long working hours and the high cost of children’s education among the causes. In 2024 the rate rose slightly for the first time since 2015, to 0.75, but that is still less than half the replacement level.

question: What is the average fertility rate in Sub-Saharan Africa today — how many children per woman?
indicator: Total fertility rate (Sub-Saharan Africa, children per woman)
why: From the 1960s to the mid-1980s a woman in the region had between 6.5 and 6.8 children on average (peaking at 6.81 in the late 1970s). Since then it has been falling, and over the past two decades ever faster: from 5.52 in 2006 to 4.94 in 2015 and 4.26 in 2024. Still, the region is on this path later than others: 4.26 is the level the world as a whole had in 1974.

question: How many children does a woman in the world have on average?
indicator: Total fertility rate (world, children per woman)
why: In 1950 a woman in the world had 4.85 children on average; in 2023, 2.25. As more children survive to adulthood, parents no longer need many births to be sure some will grow up, and where family planning is within reach most choose to have fewer. The fall was uneven: in the 2000s it almost stalled (2.68 in 2002, 2.57 in 2013) and only then sped up again. Fewer is not better without limit: where the rate drops far below two, populations age and shrink. And the rate is a snapshot of one year’s birth rates, not a tally of real families.

question: On average, how much fertiliser does a hectare of arable land get in China?
indicator: Fertiliser consumption (China, kg of plant nutrients per hectare of arable land)
why: China is the world’s largest fertiliser user, and for decades fields received more fertiliser than crops can take up, while the surplus nitrogen and phosphorus polluted rivers, lakes and air. In 2015 the government adopted a plan to stop the growth of fertiliser use by 2020. After the 2016 peak (481 kg per hectare) use fell to 393 kg in 2024, while cereal yields rose from 6.02 to 6.49 tonnes per hectare. The plan’s goal has been met, but per-hectare use is still higher than in 2005 (378 kg).

question: How many kilograms of fertiliser are applied per hectare of arable land in Sub-Saharan Africa?
indicator: Fertiliser consumption (Sub-Saharan Africa, kg of plant nutrients per hectare of arable land)
why: Without nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, soils wear out and harvests fall. By 1981 fertiliser use in the region had risen to 17.7 kg per hectare, then it fell for a quarter of a century, to 11 kg in 2005. In 2006 African Union countries set a goal of 50 kg by 2015. Use has risen since, to 22.8 kg in 2020, but in 2023 it was only 19.3 kg, about seven times less than the world average (136.5 kg).

question: What was the death rate from fires and burns in Africa in 2021, per 100,000 people?
indicator: Death rate from fire, heat and hot substances (Africa, deaths per 100,000 people)
why: Over twenty years Africa’s death rate from fires and burns changed little: 3.50 per 100,000 in 2000 and 3.28 in 2021. At the start of the century Europe’s rate was almost the same, 3.31, and by 2021 it had fallen to 1.34, so the gap between the continents is not a fixed fact. Among the risk factors WHO names cooking over open fires and on unstable stoves; two-thirds of the world’s burn deaths occur in WHO’s African and South-East Asia regions.

question: How many people per 100,000 in Estonia died from fire and burns in 2021?
indicator: Death rate from fire, heat and hot substances (Estonia, deaths per 100,000 people)
why: Estonia stands out for the steepness of its decline: between 2006 and 2009 the death rate from fire and burns fell from 12.4 to 5.1 per 100,000, and by 2021 to 2.6. Smoke detectors have been mandatory in residential buildings since 2009, and the Rescue Board credits general prevention work and the growing use of detectors: before they were mandatory, fires took close to 200 lives a year; in 2024 they took 34, the lowest on record. But neighbouring Finland’s rate in 2021 was 0.83 per 100,000, a third of Estonia’s.

question: What share of the world’s marine fish stocks is overfished?

The wild catch from seas and inland waters has not grown for almost 30 years: 96.4 million tonnes in 1996 and 94.4 million in 2024. Where catches are strictly limited by quotas, stocks recover, but there are still too few such cases to turn the global figure around.

question: How many fixed broadband connections are there per 100 people worldwide?

question: How many people per 100,000 died in floods worldwide each year in the 2010s, on average over the decade?
indicator: Death rate from floods (world, decade average, deaths per 100,000 people per year)
why: In the 2010s floods killed on average 0.069 people per 100,000 a year, 60% fewer than in the 1970s (0.175). The path was not straight: in the 1990s the rate climbed back to 0.163. Our World in Data warns that disaster records before 2000 are incomplete, so the earlier decades are more likely understated than exaggerated. question: Out of every 100 dollars of income, how many do Americans spend on groceries for eating at home?
indicator: Spending on food at home (USA, % of disposable income)
why: The US has one of the longest unbroken series of this kind, going back to 1929. Back then groceries for home cooking took a fifth of income; now they take less than a twentieth. Incomes grew and farms became more productive, so food took an ever smaller share of the budget. But Americans eat out more and more: cafés, restaurants and takeaways now take 5.5% of income, more than groceries do. Together that makes 10.4%, against 23.4% in 1929.

indicator: People in moderate or severe food insecurity (world, billions, three-year average)

Their number has grown since 2015: the share rose from 21.7% to 28.3%, and the count from 1.62 to 2.29 billion. It rose fastest until 2021 and has barely changed since. Large tree-planting programmes in several countries and forest regrowing naturally on abandoned land both contributed. question: What share of the European Union’s land is covered by forest?

question: What share of girls in low-income countries finish primary school?

question: Gravitational waves were first caught in 2015. How many black-hole mergers and other events had detectors confidently recorded by the end of 2023?

question: In 2015, 81.3% of adolescents in Latin America reached the last grade of lower secondary school. What about in 2024?

why: From 1999 to 2015 the rate rose by more than a percentage point a year, from 63.7% to 81.3%. Those years saw the spread of cash payments to poor families on condition that their children attend school: Mexico launched such a programme in 1997, Brazil its "Bolsa Família" in 2003. Since then it has plateaued: the highest value, 83.9%, came in 2021, and in 2024 it was 81.5%, about the same as in 2015. question: How many Dutch men per 100,000 died of lung cancer in 2023 (age-adjusted)?
indicator: Lung cancer death rate among men (Netherlands, per 100,000, age-standardised)
why: Lung cancer follows smoking with a lag of several decades, and the Netherlands shows the whole cycle. In the mid-20th century most Dutch men smoked, and the lung cancer death rate rose from 24.8 in 1950 to 89.3 in 1982. As men quit and smoking became more expensive and less advertised, the rate went down, reaching 27.8 in 2023. But Dutch women took up smoking in large numbers later: their death rate rose from 7.7 in 1982 to 25.8 in 2011 and only since then has it been falling — to 21.7 in 2023.

question: Are malaria deaths falling?
indicator: Malaria death rate
why: Mass rollout of insecticide-treated bed nets, rapid tests, and artemisinin treatment funded through the Global Fund cut the age-standardized death rate by about a third since its early-2000s peak. Yet malaria still kills roughly 600,000 people a year, most of them children under 5, and progress has stalled near 10 per 100,000 as drug resistance spreads.

question: How much does the world spend each year on research into new malaria drugs, vaccines and tests?
indicator: Funding for malaria research and development (world, million US dollars, 2024 prices)
why: Research on diseases of poor countries, such as malaria, is funded mostly by public agencies in rich countries and, among philanthropies, above all by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and the Wellcome Trust. These years brought the first malaria vaccines, recommended by the WHO in 2021 and 2023. But research money is not growing: since 2009 it has moved between $668 million (2022) and $818 million (2018), and in 2024 it was $736 million, about a tenth below the peak.

question: How often do people in Sri Lanka catch malaria — how many cases a year per 1,000 people living in at-risk areas?
indicator: Malaria incidence (Sri Lanka, cases per 1,000 people at risk)
value: 0 (2024) — no locally acquired cases since October 2012
why: As recently as 2000, Sri Lanka recorded 47.33 malaria cases per 1,000 people in at-risk areas. The country changed its approach: besides killing mosquitoes, it began finding and quickly treating the patients themselves — mobile clinics worked where malaria spread most, while surveillance and health education helped put out outbreaks in time. There have been no locally acquired cases since October 2012, and in 2016 WHO certified the country malaria-free. The main threat now is cases brought in from abroad: to keep the disease from returning, each one has to be found and treated in time.

question: What is the world’s death rate from starvation-level malnutrition?
indicator: Death rate from protein-energy malnutrition (world, per 100,000 people per year)
why: These are deaths from extreme wasting, when the body goes without enough energy and protein for a long time. From 2000 to 2021 the death rate fell from 6.5 to 2.5 per 100,000 people, and the number of such deaths from 399,000 to 196,000 a year (WHO’s latest estimates stop at 2021). Hunger became rarer and treatment for wasting more accessible. Yet almost 200,000 deaths a year from lack of food, in a world that grows enough of it overall, is still far too many.

question: Key Biodiversity Areas are the places on Earth that matter most for nature. On average, how much of each such area at sea is covered by protected zones?
indicator: Average share of each marine Key Biodiversity Area covered by protected areas (world)
why: In 2000 protected zones covered, on average, a quarter of each marine Key Biodiversity Area (25.7%); by 2020 it was 45.4%. Since then progress has almost stopped: 46.6% in 2023 and 46.7% in 2025. More than half of the average site still lies outside any protected area.

indicator: Marine protected areas, share of territorial waters (Chile)
why: Chile’s protected sea grew in leaps: 4.4% in 2015, 12.6% in 2016, 28.8% in 2018 and 41.2% in 2019. The largest additions were huge marine parks around remote islands, Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the Juan Fernández archipelago and the Diego Ramírez Islands, created by presidential decrees in early 2018. question: Out of every 100 square kilometres of the Seychelles’ territorial waters, how many are now marine protected areas?
indicator: Marine protected areas, share of territorial waters (Seychelles)
why: The island nation took an unusual route. In 2016, in a deal negotiated by The Nature Conservancy, part of its foreign debt was converted into a $22 million investment in marine conservation, in exchange for a plan to protect 30% of its waters. The first zones were formally designated in 2018, and in this data the share rose from zero to 15.7% in 2019 and 32.8% in 2020. But fishing and other extraction are fully banned only in some zones, such as the waters around Aldabra atoll; the rest allows sustainable use.

question: Is maternal mortality falling?
indicator: Maternal mortality
why: Skilled care during birth and access to emergency help make the most dangerous complications manageable. The global rate for 2023 is 197 per 100,000 live births, but progress has slowed to roughly 0.5% a year since 2015.

question: In how many countries does the law guarantee mothers at least 14 weeks of paid leave?
indicator: Number of countries where the law guarantees mothers at least 14 weeks of paid leave (world)
why: In 1970, 45 countries guaranteed such leave, and 77 did in 2000. Then the pace picked up: between 2015 and 2023 alone another 22 countries adopted the rule, bringing the total to 122. Yet in 68 of the 190 economies the World Bank tracks, the law still gives mothers no such guarantee. And a legal right alone does not show how many women actually use it.

question: Are people getting more schooling?
indicator: Years of schooling (adults)
why: The spread of compulsory public schooling and better-educated younger cohorts replacing older ones lifted the world average from 5.9 years in 1990 to 8.8. Yet that is still short of a completed secondary education, and in the poorest regions adults average only about 6 years.

question: How many children get the measles vaccine?
indicator: Measles vaccination (1-year-olds)
why: Routine immunization programs raised first-dose measles coverage from 13% of the world's one-year-olds to 84%. But measles is contagious enough to need about 95%: coverage dipped during COVID and has not fully recovered, and outbreaks have returned where it slipped.

question: How much meat does the world produce in a year?
indicator: Meat production (world, million tonnes)
why: The world produces five times as much meat as in 1961: 374 million tonnes against 71 million. The population grew too, but even per person there is now almost twice as much meat, 45 kg a year against 23. For many people that means more protein in their diet. But livestock is one of the largest sources of methane and needs vast areas for pasture and feed, so this growth comes at a high cost to the climate and to nature.

question: How much methane does the world emit in a year (in CO₂ terms)?
indicator: Methane emissions (world, billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent per year over a 100-year horizon, including land use)
why: In the 1990s methane emissions barely changed: 7.32 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent in 1990 and 7.54 billion in 2000. Since then they have risen almost every year, reaching 9.50 billion tonnes in 2024. In 2021, at the COP26 climate summit, the EU and the United States launched the Global Methane Pledge: to cut global methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030. So far the movement is the other way: from 8.90 billion tonnes in 2020 to 9.50 billion in 2024, 7% more.

question: What is India’s annual milk output?
indicator: Milk production, all milking animals (India, million tonnes)
why: India is the world’s largest milk producer: 248 million tonnes in 2024, about a quarter of the world total (985 million tonnes). In the 1960s it produced about 20 million tonnes, and output was not growing. In 1970 the government launched Operation Flood: millions of small farmers joined village dairy cooperatives that collected milk every day and shipped it to the cities. Yet milk per animal rose only 2.9 times (from 530 to 1,539 kg a year), so much of the growth came from more animals, which need more feed, water and pasture.

question: How much plastic waste a year is burned in the open, dumped into water or unmanaged dumps, or simply littered worldwide?
indicator: Mismanaged plastic waste: burned in the open, dumped into water or unmanaged dumps, or littered (world, million tonnes per year)
why: Recycling grew fastest of all the ways plastic waste is handled: from 5.8 million tonnes in 2000 to 32.8 million in 2019, that is, from under 4 to over 9 tonnes in every 100 tonnes of plastic waste. The mismanaged share fell slightly, from 26 to 22.5 tonnes in every 100. But the waste itself more than doubled, from 156 to 353 million tonnes, so the plastic that ends up in the environment or burns with no controls almost doubled too: 79.3 million tonnes against 40.6 million.

indicator: Population covered by 4G mobile networks

But coverage isn’t use: only 73.6% of people use the internet (ITU, 2025) — the cost of a smartphone and data and a lack of skills hold many back — and more than 7% of people still live beyond 4G reach.

Agent networks built by telecom operators lifted the share of adults with such an account from 11.4% to 40% in ten years — 2.5 times the world average (16%). indicator: Own a mobile phone (people aged 10+, world)

indicator: Number of countries that are parties to the Nagoya Protocol on access to genetic resources and benefit-sharing (world)
why: The protocol was adopted in Nagoya, Japan, in 2010 as an addition to the Convention on Biological Diversity. The benefits can be money, such as royalties, or shared research results. At first countries joined quickly: 23 in 2016 alone, from 69 to 92. Then the pace slowed: 137 in 2022, 139 in 2023 and 141 in 2024, and in 2025 the count did not change.

question: In 1965, at the height of the Apollo programme, NASA’s budget was $34 billion in 2020 dollars. What about in 2022?
indicator: NASA annual budget (United States, billion US dollars, 2020 prices)
why: NASA’s budget is a public space-research spending series more than 60 years long, and it shows how a government’s willingness to pay for this research changes. At the height of the Moon programme, in 1966, NASA received 4.4% of all US federal spending. After Apollo its budget fell, and since the late 1980s it has stayed at roughly $18–25 billion a year in 2020 dollars, while its share of federal spending shrank to about 0.5% in 2013. Since the 2013 low ($19 billion) the budget has been rising slowly, to $24.8 billion in 2022, but it is still more than a quarter below 1965.

indicator: Deaths from natural disasters

question: How many asteroids between 140 metres and 1 kilometre across, on orbits that come close to Earth, are known?
indicator: Known near-Earth asteroids 140 m to 1 km across (world, cumulative)
why: In 2005 the US Congress told NASA to find 90% of near-Earth objects 140 metres or larger by 2020. Survey telescopes grew the catalogue of asteroids between 140 m and 1 km from 466 in 2000 to 10,624 in 2025. The big ones, over a kilometre, are nearly all known (877 in 2025): their 90% goal was met back in 2011. But for all near-Earth asteroids of 140 m and up the goal has not been met: estimates put the share found at between 38% (a 2023 estimate) and about half (2021).

question: What share of young people in Turkey (aged 15–24) are not in education, employment or training?
indicator: Share of young people aged 15–24 not in education, employment or training (Turkey)
why: The biggest change has been among young women: in 2000, 56.8% of them were neither studying nor working; in 2025, 30.9% were. Among young men the figures were 21.8% and 16.3%. In 2012 Turkey extended compulsory schooling from 8 to 12 years, so adolescents stay in school longer. But the decline was not smooth: in 2019–2020 the share rose back to 28.3%, and among young women it is still almost twice as high as among men.

question: Is neonatal mortality falling?
indicator: Neonatal mortality (first 28 days)
why: Skilled birth attendance, basic antiseptics, and newborn care made the first weeks of life far safer — the global rate fell from 37 to 17 per 1,000 live births between 1990 and 2024. But progress here trails older children: neonatal deaths now make up 47% of all under-5 deaths, meaning 2.3 million newborns still die in their first month every year.

question: How often is newborn tetanus reported worldwide — how many cases per million people?
indicator: Reported cases of neonatal tetanus (world, per million people)
why: A newborn catches tetanus through the umbilical stump when the cord is cut with an unclean instrument; without hospital care most infected babies die. Vaccinating the mother before birth and clean delivery protect against it. In 1990, 4.75 cases per million people were reported; by 2018, 0.23. Since then the decline has stopped: the rate jumps from year to year and was 0.52 in 2024. And reported cases are only part of the real ones: where women give birth at home, cases often go unreported.

question: Are fewer people getting HIV?
indicator: New HIV infections
why: Condoms, antiretroviral treatment that makes the virus undetectable and non-transmissible, PrEP, and harm-reduction programs for people who inject drugs cut new HIV infections by 65% from the 1995 peak (3.5 million a year) — but progress has been uneven: the total barely moved from 2010 to 2015 (2.1 million both years), and the 1.2 million new infections in 2025 are still more than three times the UN’s 2025 target of under 370,000.

question: How many people worldwide need treatment or prevention for neglected tropical diseases?
indicator: People requiring interventions against neglected tropical diseases (world, billion)
why: Neglected tropical diseases are some twenty diseases of poverty, from trachoma, which causes blindness, to elephantiasis and intestinal worms. WHO counts the people who need mass preventive treatment or care. From 2010 to 2024 their number fell by 780 million, from 2.19 to 1.41 billion: drug companies donate the medicines for mass treatment free of charge, and more and more countries are getting rid of individual diseases altogether. Yet between 2016 and 2020 the number barely moved (1.76 and 1.73 billion), and WHO’s goal for 2030 is 90% fewer people needing such interventions.

indicator: Oil’s share of electricity generation (world)

question: What share of children with diarrhoea in South Asia receive oral rehydration salts?
indicator: Children under 5 with diarrhoea who received an oral rehydration salts packet (South Asia)
why: Diarrhoea is still one of the leading causes of death in children under five, and the simplest treatment is a packet of oral rehydration salts: a mix of salts and glucose dissolved in clean water to replace the fluid the body has lost. In 1993, 17.7% of sick children in South Asia got such a packet; in 2021, 60.6%, as health workers began handing out the packets. Yet four in ten sick children still go without.

question: Out of every 100 baht spent on health in Thailand, how many do people pay out of their own pockets?

question: In 2000, 48.7 million girls of lower-secondary-school age worldwide were not in school. How many were there in 2025?

question: How many people went to space between 1961 and 2020?

question: What quantity of pesticides is used, on average, per hectare of cropland worldwide?
indicator: Pesticide use (world, kg of active ingredients per hectare of cropland)
why: Pesticides protect crops from pests, weeds and disease, but they can harm pollinating insects, soil life and water. Since 1990 their use per hectare worldwide has almost doubled, from 1.23 to 2.40 kg. It can be cut: since 2014 China has reduced pesticide use per hectare by a third, from 2.59 to 1.71 kg (2023). question: In 2003 Brazilian 15-year-olds scored 356 in PISA maths. What did they score in 2018?
indicator: Mean PISA mathematics score, 15-year-old students (Brazil)
why: From 2003 to 2012 Brazilian 15-year-olds raised their maths score by 35 points, to 391, making Brazil one of the biggest improvers in PISA over those years. In 2007 the country introduced a national education quality index: every school got targets checked by tests. After 2012 the rise stopped: 377 in 2015, 384 in 2018, and in 2022 girls scored 375 and boys 383. Brazil is still more than 100 points below the OECD average (489 in 2018).

question: What was the average PISA maths score of Finnish 15-year-olds in 2018?

question: How many samples of food and farm plants do the world’s genebanks hold?
indicator: Samples of plant genetic resources for food and agriculture stored in genebanks (world, millions)
why: Genebanks store seeds and other plant material of the crops and species that feed humanity, as insurance in case they are lost in the field. Their collections have almost doubled, from 3.11 million samples in 1995 to 5.99 million in 2024. But growth has slowed sharply: 1.91 million samples were added in 1995–2010, and only 0.19 million in 2019–2024.

question: How much plastic did the world produce in 2019?
indicator: Plastic production — polymer resins and fibres (world, million tonnes per year)
why: In 1950 the world produced 2 million tonnes of plastic, in 1970 35 million, in 2000 213 million, and in 2019 460 million tonnes, more than twice as much as at the turn of the century. question: What is the average concentration of fine PM2.5 particles in the air people breathe in Poland?
indicator: Fine PM2.5 particles in the air (Poland, population-weighted average, urban and rural, µg/m³)
why: The average concentration of fine PM2.5 particles breathed by people in Poland fell from 32.3 µg/m³ in 1990 to 16.5 in 2023, almost by half. Polish cities and regions are restricting the burning of coal and wood in old stoves and boilers: in Kraków it has been banned outright since September 2019. Since 2020 the level has changed little. question: In 2000, 2.68 people per 100,000 in Europe and Central Asia died from accidental poisoning. What was the rate in 2021?
indicator: Death rate from unintentional poisoning (Europe and Central Asia, World Bank region, deaths per 100,000 people; excludes alcohol poisoning and most drug overdoses)
why: In twenty years Europe and Central Asia cut its death rate from accidental poisoning by almost two-thirds, from 2.68 to 0.95 per 100,000, though the statistics themselves do not explain why the decline was so steep. indicator: Death rate from unintentional poisoning (world, deaths per 100,000 people; excludes alcohol poisoning and most drug overdoses)
why: Since peaking in 2003 at 1.10 per 100,000, the world’s death rate from accidental poisoning has been falling, reaching 0.75 in 2021. This UN Sustainable Development Goals indicator counts poisoning by household chemicals, pesticides, kerosene, carbon monoxide and medicines; accidental alcohol poisoning and most drug overdoses are not included. question: Has polio been eradicated?
indicator: Polio (wild virus)
why: Vaccination narrowed endemic spread to two countries, but reaching zero means holding coverage — 2023 (12 cases) was a record low, then cases jumped to 99 in 2024 (Afghanistan and Pakistan) before easing back to 40 in 2025, still 3x above the 2023 low.

question: In total, how far short of $3 a day do the world’s extremely poor fall each year?
indicator: Total shortfall from the $3-a-day line (world, billion 2021 dollars a year, adjusted for inflation and living costs)
why: Add up how much each extremely poor person falls short of $3 a day and you get the sum that would have to be redistributed every year so that no one is left below the line. Rising incomes shrank it from $1,025 billion in 1990 to $303 billion in 2017. Since then it has barely moved: $324 billion in 2021 and $313 billion in 2024, less than 0.2% of world GDP. The real cost would be higher, because money cannot reach everyone without costs and losses.

question: What share of the world’s people live on less than $8.30 a day?
indicator: Share of people living on less than $8.30 a day (world, 2021 dollars adjusted for inflation and living costs)
why: $8.30 a day is the poverty line the World Bank uses for upper-middle-income countries: no longer extreme poverty, but far from comfort. In the 1990s more than 70% of humanity lived below it, and the share barely moved for a decade. Since then growing economies and earnings have brought it down to 46.2% in 2024. Still, almost half the world lives below this line, and since 2019 (49.6%) the share has been falling more slowly than in the five years before.

question: What is the world’s pre-primary enrolment rate (as a percentage of children of pre-school age)?
indicator: Gross enrolment ratio, pre-primary education (world)
why: In 1970 the number of children enrolled in pre-primary education worldwide equalled only about one in six children of pre-school age. Enrolment grew fastest from the mid-2000s, from 39.6% in 2006 to 60.9% in 2020, as many countries made at least one year of pre-school free or compulsory. Early learning helps children do better at school later. But this is a gross ratio: it counts enrolled children, not how much time they spend in class or what they learn there.

question: Out of every 100 thirty-year-olds worldwide, how many will die before 70 from heart disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic lung disease?
indicator: Probability of dying between ages 30 and 70 from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease (world)
why: These four groups of diseases are the main causes of death in middle age. The probability of dying from them between 30 and 70 fell from 22.6% in 2000 to 18.3% in 2021, helped by less smoking, drugs for blood pressure and cholesterol, and earlier detection of cancer. But progress has slowed: since 2015 the rate has dropped only from 18.9% to 18.3%. UN countries set a goal of cutting this premature mortality by a third from its 2015 level by 2030, to about 12.6% — at the current pace it will not be met.

question: Out of every 100 primary-school pupils in the world, how many are repeating a grade?
indicator: Repeaters as a share of primary-school enrolment (world)
why: In 1970 almost one primary-school pupil in ten in the world was repeating a grade; in 2018 it was about three in a hundred. A repeated year costs the school and the family one more year of schooling, and the child ends up among younger classmates. Many countries have limited grade repetition, especially in the first grades. But fewer repeaters does not mean better learning: where pupils are promoted automatically, the gaps simply move up to the next grade.

question: What share of primary schools in India have internet for teaching?
indicator: Primary schools with internet for teaching (India)
why: India has one of the world’s largest school systems, so the change here is vast: in six years the share of primary schools with internet for teaching rose more than eightfold, from 6.4% in 2019 to 54.3% in 2025. Cheaper connectivity and government efforts to digitise schools helped. Still, almost half of India’s primary schools have no internet for teaching.

question: What share of the world’s primary schools have internet for teaching?
indicator: Primary schools with internet for teaching (world)
why: Governments are connecting schools, and initiatives such as Giga (UNICEF and ITU) help map unconnected ones and negotiate with providers; progress sped up after 2021, from 39.7% to 48%. But over eight years the share rose only 11 percentage points, and about half of the world’s primary schools still have no internet for teaching.

question: In 1970 the world had 15.8 million primary-school teachers. How many were there in 2024?
indicator: Primary-school teachers (world)
why: In half a century the number of primary-school teachers in the world more than doubled, to 34.1 million in 2024. Teachers were added faster than pupils: in 1970 there were on average 28.1 pupils per teacher, in 2018, 23.4. Fewer pupils per teacher means more time for each child. But this is only a headcount: it does not show what training these teachers have or whether they work where they are most needed.

question: What share of the world’s forests lies within legally established protected areas?
indicator: Share of forest area within legally established protected areas (world)
why: National parks, nature reserves and other protected areas cover more and more forest: in 1990 they contained 12.9% of the world’s forests, in 2025 19.3%. The share grew fastest in 2000–2010 (from 14.4% to 17.4%), while in 2015–2025 it added only a little over one percentage point. The figure is about status on paper, not about how well protection is enforced on the ground. And about four in every five hectares of forest remain outside such areas.

question: What share of the Earth’s land has protected-area status?
indicator: Share of land area within protected areas (world)
why: National parks, nature reserves and other protected areas covered 15% of the world’s land in 2013 and 16.5% in 2025; in 2016 the share even dipped to 14.9%. In December 2022 the parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity adopted the Kunming-Montreal framework, which aims to conserve at least 30% of land and sea by 2030. At the pace of 2013–2025, about 0.1 percentage points a year, that goal is out of reach: protected land would have to almost double in five years.

question: The Protein Data Bank (PDB) collects experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins and other molecules. How many did it hold in 2023?
indicator: Experimentally determined 3D molecular structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB), thousand entries
why: The open Protein Data Bank, founded in 1971, collects structures determined by experiment: mostly X-ray crystallography, also NMR and, since 2013, increasingly cryo-electron microscopy. Between 1990 and 2023 its entries grew more than 400-fold, from 507 to 212,599. These experiments are expensive and slow, so structures are now also predicted: the AlphaFold database already held 214.7 million models in 2022. But a prediction is not a measurement: AlphaFold models single protein chains rather than the complexes they form, and parts of them with low confidence.

question: How many passenger-kilometres are travelled by rail in France each year?
indicator: Rail passenger travel (France, billion passenger-kilometres per year)
why: In 1981 France opened its first high-speed TGV line, between Paris and Lyon, and trains began to compete with planes and cars. Rail travel more than doubled: from 41 billion passenger-kilometres in 1970 to a record 118 billion in 2022, despite a slump to 65 billion in the pandemic year 2020. But the French still travel more than seven times as far by road: 868 billion passenger-kilometres.

question: How many passenger-kilometres are travelled by rail in South Korea each year?
indicator: Rail passenger travel (South Korea, billion passenger-kilometres per year)
why: As its economy grew, South Korea also built up its railways: trains carried 10 billion passenger-kilometres in 1970 and 45 billion in 1991. question: How many countries had joined the Ramsar Convention on wetlands by 2015?
indicator: Number of parties to the Ramsar Convention on wetlands (world)
why: The convention protecting marshes, lakes, floodplains and other wetlands was signed in the Iranian town of Ramsar in 1971 and came into force in 1975, with 7 parties. By 2015 there were 169, and the data in this series ends there. But membership is a commitment, not a measurement: the number of parties says nothing about how much wetland has actually been saved.

question: What share of its GDP does Egypt put into research and development?
indicator: Spending on research and development, share of GDP (Egypt; all sectors combined)
why: Egypt wrote research funding into its constitution: Article 23 of the 2014 Constitution requires the state to allocate government spending of no less than 1% of gross national product to scientific research. Total R&D spending rose from 0.43% of GDP in 2009 to 0.64% in 2014 and 1.02% in 2022. But it has plateaued since (1.02% again in 2024), and this measure counts all sectors together, so it does not test the constitutional rule on government spending itself.

question: The "Europe 2020" strategy set the EU a target of spending 3% of GDP on research and development. How much was the EU spending in 2023?
indicator: Spending on research and development, share of GDP (EU-27)
why: The EU wrote its target of 3% of GDP for research and development into the "Europe 2020" strategy, which followed the Lisbon Strategy of 2000–2010. The share did rise: from 1.7% in 1996 to 1.96% in 2010 and 2.21% in 2019. But it never reached 3%: 2.26% in 2023, only slightly above 2019.

question: In 2009 Finland put 3.73% of its GDP into research and development. What about in 2023?
indicator: Spending on research and development, share of GDP (Finland)
why: Finland shows how a whole country’s research can hinge on one company. According to an IMF working paper, Nokia’s research in Finland in 2008 made up about half of all business R&D spending in the country and 37% of its total R&D spending. When Nokia’s crisis began in 2008 and it left the phone market in 2014, R&D fell from 3.73% of GDP (2009) to 2.75% (2016). It has been recovering slowly since — 3.09% in 2023 — but is still well short of the peak.

question: Out of every dollar the world economy earns, how many cents go to research and development?
indicator: Spending on research and development, share of GDP (world; business, government, universities and non-profits combined)
why: For almost twenty years, from 1996 to 2013, the world spent about 2% of GDP on research and development: science got more money only because the economy itself grew. After 2013 the share moved up — 2.26% in 2019 and 2.6% in 2023, with a visible step in 2020 — so over the decade research spending grew faster than GDP. But that is a rise of only 0.6 percentage points in a decade, and it is an average: it says nothing about how the money is spread across countries.

question: Europe’s Red List Index has been falling since the late 1990s. Where was it in 2025?
indicator: Red List Index: extinction risk of species (Europe; 1 = all species of least concern, 0 = all extinct)
why: Europe’s index fell from 0.93 in the mid-1990s to 0.89 in 2006 and 0.84 in 2025, and it has not risen in any year since. The index tracks threat categories, not numbers of animals, so it shows that more European species have moved closer to extinction than away from it. Its earliest years are an estimate: before a group of species was first assessed, the index is extended backwards in a straight line.

question: What share of all the energy the Netherlands consumes comes from renewable sources?
indicator: Renewable energy share of total final energy consumption (Netherlands)
why: In a 2018 Ipsos survey (about 500 people aged 16–64 in the Netherlands), those asked guessed on average that 22% of the country’s energy was renewable; in 2018 it was 7.4%. For decades the share grew slowly: 1.6% in 1999, 4.9% in 2012. question: How much rice does one hectare of field yield in Bangladesh?

question: How many people died on Japan’s roads in 2022?
indicator: Road traffic deaths per year (Japan)
why: Japan shows how far road deaths can be cut in half a century: 21,795 people died in road crashes in 1970 and 3,216 in 2022, almost seven times fewer. question: How many boys are born in South Korea for every 100 girls?
indicator: Sex ratio at birth (South Korea, boys per 100 girls)
why: Naturally about 105 boys are born for every 100 girls. In South Korea in the 1980s and early 1990s families wanted fewer children but insisted on a son, and when an ultrasound showed a girl, some pregnancies were ended: in 1994, 117.1 boys were born per 100 girls. A 1987 law banned doctors from telling parents the sex of the foetus, but researchers find that the main change was a weakening of son preference itself, as people moved to cities and more women got an education. By 2015 the ratio was back to natural. Elsewhere it is still skewed: in China, 110.6 in 2023.

question: How many new cases of sleeping sickness did DR Congo report in 2024?

why: Sleeping sickness is spread by tsetse flies; untreated, it attacks the brain and is usually fatal. DR Congo accounts for most of the world’s cases, so it is where you can see whether the disease is being overcome. In the 1990s, when mass screening lapsed, cases rose to 26,318 in 1998. Since then mobile teams have screened villages, simpler drugs have arrived — including fexinidazole tablets, which need no hospital drip — and flies are caught with insecticide traps. In 2024, 330 cases were reported. But only the patients who are found get counted, so the search has to go on even as cases become rare.

question: In 1979 the world released 141 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the air. How much in 2022?

why: Sulphur dioxide is released when coal and other sulphur-containing fuels are burned, and it is one of the main causes of acid rain. Since then they have fallen faster: power stations fitted equipment that strips sulphur from their smoke, and fuels became lower in sulphur. indicator: Stillbirth rate (world, per 1,000 total births, from 28 weeks of pregnancy)
why: A stillbirth is the death of a baby in the womb late in pregnancy or during labour; for a long time they were barely counted and rarely talked about. Since 2000 the rate has fallen from 22.6 to 14.3 per 1,000 births, thanks to better care during pregnancy, skilled attendants at birth and timely caesarean sections. question: In 1951 stomach cancer killed 54 in every 100,000 people in Japan (age-adjusted). How many in 2023?
indicator: Stomach cancer death rate (Japan, per 100,000, age-standardised)
why: Japan long had one of the world’s highest stomach cancer death rates. Each new generation was less likely to pick up the main cause of the disease, the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, thanks to clean water and better hygiene, and as refrigerators spread people ate less salted and pickled food. The country also introduced mass stomach screening early, so cancers are more often found at an early stage. In 2023 the death rate was 8.2 — still far higher than, for example, in the United States (1.8 in 2022).

question: Cyclones in Bangladesh: how many people per 100,000 died in storms each year in the 2010s, on average over the decade?
indicator: Death rate from storms and cyclones (Bangladesh, decade average, deaths per 100,000 people per year)
why: Bangladesh shows what preparedness can do. After Cyclone Bhola, the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society set up the Cyclone Preparedness Programme: it now has 76,000 volunteers, half of them women, and the country has more than 14,000 cyclone shelters. In the 2010s storms killed on average 0.037 people per 100,000 a year, more than a thousand times fewer than in the 1970s (44.4), though in the 1990s the rate was still 12.5. But there are still not enough cyclone shelters for the 35 million people living near the coast, and after Cyclone Amphan in 2020, which killed 26 people, families lost crops and cattle much as before: saving lives has improved faster than saving livelihoods.

question: How much tree cover did Indonesia lose in 2024?
indicator: Tree-cover loss — trees over 5 m tall, from any cause (Indonesia, million hectares per year)
why: Indonesia has some of the largest tropical forests in the world. After the big fires of 2015, tree-cover loss here peaked at 2.42 million hectares in 2016. The government then strengthened the protection of peatlands and fire prevention, and in 2019 it made permanent a moratorium (in place since 2011) on new permits to clear primary forest or convert peatland. By 2021 losses had fallen to 0.84 million hectares, but then they rose again: 1.39 million in 2023 and 1.12 million in 2024. Satellite detection improved in 2011–2015, so part of the rise since 2001 may come from better counting.

question: Are tuberculosis deaths falling?
indicator: Tuberculosis death rate
why: Standardized diagnosis, free rifampicin-based treatment, and combined TB and HIV care scaled across low-income countries cut the death rate by roughly two-thirds since 2000. Yet tuberculosis still kills about 1.2 million people a year, and drug-resistant strains and millions of undiagnosed cases remain.

question: In 2009 the world spent $736 million (in 2024 prices) on tuberculosis research and development. What about in 2024?
indicator: Funding for tuberculosis research and development (world, million US dollars, 2024 prices)
why: Funding for tuberculosis research has risen by 18% since 2009, to $872 million in 2024, coming mainly from public research agencies and philanthropic foundations. New medicines followed: in late 2012 the US approved bedaquiline, the first new TB drug in more than 40 years. After $860 million in 2019, funding fell to $771 million in 2022 and only in 2024 rose past the 2019 level.

question: How fully do the world’s health systems cover essential services — on a scale from 0 to 100?

why: The WHO and World Bank index combines 14 indicators into one number: child vaccination, care in pregnancy and family planning, treatment of HIV and tuberculosis, bed nets against malaria, control of blood pressure and diabetes, and the numbers of health workers and hospital beds. From 2000 to 2015 it rose from 54 to 68, mainly thanks to wider treatment of infectious diseases. But over the next eight years the index gained only three points, to 71, and full coverage for the world is still far off.

question: How many million people in Sub-Saharan Africa are chronically undernourished?
indicator: Number of chronically undernourished people (Sub-Saharan Africa, millions)
why: Until 2009 the number of undernourished people in the region was slowly falling, from 171 to 156 million. Since then it has grown by 78%, to 278 million in 2024. The share is still below 2000 (22.3% against 26.1%), but it has been rising again since 2014 (17.8%), and with fast population growth the number has grown even faster. question: What is the unemployment rate in Poland?
indicator: Unemployment rate (Poland, % of the labour force, ILO modelled estimate)
why: After the switch to a market economy, unemployment in Poland stayed high for years and reached 20.2% in 2002: one in five of those working or looking for work had no job. After Poland joined the EU in 2004 it fell fast, although it rose again after the global financial crisis, to 10.3% in 2013. In 2025 Poland’s unemployment rate was 3%, half the EU average (5.9%).

question: What share of the world’s labour force is unemployed?
indicator: Unemployment rate (world, % of the labour force, ILO modelled estimate)
why: World unemployment rose to 6.5% in 2003 and jumped to 6.6% in pandemic-hit 2020, but then fell quickly: 4.8% in 2025 is the lowest since 1991, when the ILO estimates begin. The measure has a limit, though: only people without work who are looking for it count as unemployed. In poor countries few can afford not to work at all, so low unemployment there does not yet mean decent work.

question: In 1900 only one country gave all adults, men and women alike, the legal right to vote. How many countries did in 2025?
indicator: Number of countries where all adult men and women have the right to vote (world)
why: At the start of the 20th century voters were mostly men, and not all of them. By 1920, 19 countries had universal suffrage, and the number grew fastest in the 1950s and 1960s, reaching 111 in 1960. Part of the rise is newly independent states, which is why this counts countries rather than a share. In 2025, 6 countries had no universal suffrage. And the right to vote is not yet a free election: it says who may vote, not whether the votes are counted fairly.

question: Out of every 100 people held in prisons and detention worldwide, how many have not yet been sentenced?
indicator: Unsentenced detainees as a share of all people held in detention (world)
why: The UN tracks this figure under its goal of equal access to justice for all: a person awaiting trial is presumed innocent until proven guilty and should not be held in custody unnecessarily. In two decades the share has barely changed: lowest at 28.3% in 2011, highest at 31.7% in 2021, and 30.9% in 2024. That means almost one detainee in three worldwide is still waiting for a verdict behind bars.

question: Out of every 100 Portuguese aged 25 and over, how many have at least completed upper secondary education?

why: In the late 1990s only about one adult in seven in Portugal had completed upper secondary school: for a long time compulsory schooling there lasted only a few years, with nine years made compulsory in 1986 and twelve in 2009. Since then older generations have gradually been replaced by better-educated younger ones, and some adults earned their diploma in adult-education programmes. In 26 years the share more than tripled, to 48.6% in 2024. Even so, slightly more than half of Portuguese aged 25 and over have not completed upper secondary school.

question: What is the average concentration of fine PM2.5 particles in the air of China’s cities?
indicator: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in urban air (China, population-weighted average, µg/m³)
why: In 2013, when the average PM2.5 level in China’s cities reached 63.9 µg/m³, the government adopted a national action plan to clean the air: it limited coal burning and tightened standards for factories and cars. By 2022 the level had more than halved, to 29.7 µg/m³. But in 2023 it rose again, to 32.1.

question: What is the average concentration of fine PM2.5 particles in the air of the world’s cities?
indicator: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in urban air (world, population-weighted average, µg/m³)
why: Filters at power plants and factories, cleaner engines and stricter fuel standards have reduced urban air pollution: the average concentration of fine PM2.5 particles breathed by the world’s city dwellers fell from 36.6 µg/m³ in 2010 to 27.3 in 2023. question: What share of the world’s city dwellers live in slums?
indicator: Share of the urban population living in slums (world)
why: The UN counts a home as a slum home if it lacks at least one basic condition: water, sanitation, enough living space, solid walls or secure tenure. Water mains, sewers and sturdier houses are slowly changing poor neighbourhoods, and the share of city dwellers living in slums fell from 30.6% in 2000 to 24.8% in 2024. question: How many kilograms of vegetables a year are there per person worldwide?
indicator: Vegetables available for consumption (world, kg per person per year)
why: Until the late 1980s the world added almost no vegetables per person: 59–76 kg a year. Then came rapid growth, and now there are 147 kg for everyone. But the average hides big differences: in China there are 413 kg of vegetables per person a year, almost three times the world average. And this is supply, not what is eaten: some vegetables spoil or are thrown away.

question: Thefts of and from vehicles in England and Wales: how many thousand were there in 2025?
indicator: Vehicle-related theft: theft of and from vehicles, including attempts (England and Wales, thousands a year, household survey)
why: Until 1993 vehicle-related theft in England and Wales rose faster than ever, then it began to fall sharply. A UK Home Office study links the turning point to a “second wave” of security: central locking, car alarms and, most importantly, electronic immobilisers, mandatory on new cars from 1998. The authors caution that security did not work everywhere and is unlikely to have been the only factor. In 2018 such thefts rose again, from 787,000 to 918,000, and stayed near that level until 2020; by 2025 there were 666,000, less than a sixth of the peak.

question: After the moratorium of the 1980s Japan did not stop whaling. How many whales did it catch in 2024?
indicator: Whales caught by Japan per year
why: When the moratorium on commercial whaling took effect, Japan’s catch fell from 1,941 whales in 1985 and 2,769 in 1986 to 241 in 1988. But the country went on whaling under scientific research permits, and by 2005 the catch had climbed to 1,243. In 2014 the International Court of Justice ruled that its Antarctic programme was not scientific, and the catch dipped to 196 that year before rising again. After leaving the International Whaling Commission, since 2019 Japan has hunted only in its own waters and no longer goes to the Antarctic: 270–335 whales a year, including 30 fin whales in 2024.

question: How many whales were caught worldwide in the decade 2010–2019?
indicator: Whales caught per decade (world; from the 1990s including Indigenous subsistence hunting)
why: Industrial whaling peaked in the 1960s: 703,000 whales in a decade, about 70,000 a year. In 1982 the International Whaling Commission adopted a moratorium on commercial whaling, and from the mid-1980s catch limits were set to zero. The low came in the 1990s, 10,300 whales; in the 2000s the catch rose again to 18,141. In the 2010s 14,957 whales were caught, about 2% of the 1960s level, and that figure already includes Indigenous subsistence hunting, which the data before 1990 leaves out. Japan, Norway and Iceland still hunt whales commercially, and Indigenous hunting continues: 6,218 whales were caught in 2020–2024.

question: How many tonnes of wheat per hectare did the UK harvest in 2024?

Since then growth has stopped: from the mid-1990s yields have mostly stayed between 7 and 9 tonnes, and in 2024 they were 7.28.

question: In 2003 Morocco scored 44.4 out of 100 on the World Bank’s Women, Business and the Law index. What was its score in 2023?
indicator: Women, Business and the Law index: equality of women’s and men’s economic rights in law (Morocco; 100 = full equality)
why: More than two thirds of the gain came in a single year. In 2004 Morocco’s parliament unanimously adopted a new family code: the family became the joint responsibility of husband and wife instead of the husband alone, the minimum marriage age for women was raised to 18, and women gained the right to initiate divorce, now handled by the courts. That year the index jumped from 44.4 to 70.6. Since then the changes have been small, 73.1 in 2010 and 75.6 from 2018, and almost a quarter of the way to legal equality remains.

question: The World Bank’s Women, Business and the Law index is 100 when the law gives women the same economic rights as men. What was the average score of the world’s countries in 2023?
indicator: Women, Business and the Law index: equality of women’s and men’s economic rights in law (average of the world’s countries; 100 = full equality)
why: The index has eight parts: mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, entrepreneurship, assets and pensions. In 1970 the average country scored 45.7, less than half of equality. Until 2000 the index gained about half a point a year on average, and three quarters of a point after 2000, reaching 77.9 in 2023. In other words, on average the law gives women about three quarters of the economic rights it gives men.

question: For every 100 women of university age in South Asia, how many women are enrolled in tertiary education?

question: How many hours a year does the average worker in South Korea put in?

question: What was Poland’s workplace death rate in 2023, per 100,000 employees?

why: Between 2010 and 2023 Poland’s workplace death rate fell threefold, from 3.65 to 1.19 per 100,000 employees. Construction is the telling case: according to Eurostat figures quoted in a report by the industry’s Agreement for Safety in Construction, in 2009 Poland’s building sites recorded 21.49 fatal accidents per 100,000 workers, and within a decade fatal accidents per 100,000 construction workers fell fourfold. The largest construction firms behind the agreement credit uniform safety requirements for everyone, subcontractors included, and a single mandatory safety-training system. But that is the industry’s own assessment, and Poland’s overall rate of workplace accidents rose in 2023, from 4.66 to 4.90 per 1,000 people employed.

question: In 2006 Singapore passed a new workplace safety law. Out of every 100,000 workers, how many died at work in 2024?

why: Singapore stands out because it set itself a numeric target and worked towards it. After a series of major industrial accidents, in 2006 the country passed a new Workplace Safety and Health Act, moving from a list of prescriptive rules to making companies answerable for results. But in 2024 the rate rose again to 1.17, and many accidents happen in construction and the marine sector, which employ many foreign workers.
